newsitem.title: USA: Clinton and Dole prepare for debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton and Dole prepare for debate.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Friday affected an unusually modest tone about his abilities as he and Republican Bob Dole both rehearsed intensively for Sunday's first presidential debate.

"I'm badly out of shape on this, but I'm trying to get better," a smiling, relaxed Clinton told reporters as he emerged from a lakeside hotel serving as his pre-debate headquarters to soak up the glorious autumn weather at the Chautauqua Institution, a quiet Victorian-era resort in western New York State.

Turning to former Senate Democratic leader George Mitchell, who is impersonating Dole in dress rehearsals for the Hartford, Conn. debate on Sunday night, Clinton said: "Tell the truth, George. You beat me like a drum. You kicked me all over the place last night."
Buttressing the president's effort to lower expectations, Mitchell said he probably debated Dole more than anyone else when they were in the Senate together "and I know just how effective he is."
"Senator Dole is a highly skilled debater, and I think he's going to be tough in this debate coming up on Sunday. But the president, I think, will do all right," he said.

Dole, who has been playing down his expectations for weeks, spent much of Thursday making self-deprecating jokes about the encounter that he and his aides hope will pump new life into his floundering campaign.
At one campaign event in Tennessee, Dole joked about whether he would even show up and added, "This is the biggest audience I'll ever address, at least for the first few minutes."
The Dole campaign also began airing a new advertisement blasting Clinton as a tax-and-spend liberal who tries to present himself as a centrist.
A Reuters tracking poll on Friday showed Clinton widening his lead over Dole to 14.3 percentage points. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot's support dropped to 4.4 percent, its lowest level yet.

Perot, who performed well in the 1992 debates, has been excluded this year because of his low poll ratings. The Federal Communications Commission on Friday slammed another door in his face, rejecting a request by the Texas billionaire to force big television networks to sell him more prime time for campaign commercials.
The FCC decided unanimously that the networks acted legally by refusing to sell Perot extra prime time slots for his half-hour campaign "infomercials".
With polls showing that almost 80 percent of voters think Clinton will win the Nov. 5 election, Dole badly needs to land some heavy blows on Sunday to turn the race around.

The Reuters poll showed voters giving Clinton fairly good marks for his handling of the Israeli-Palestinian crisis. Nine percent called the president's performance "excellent", 33 percent said it was "good", 29 percent said it was "fair" and 14 percent rated it "poor".
Dole has been taking the debate extremely seriously, cutting back on campaign appearances so he could practice in mock encounters in which Tennessee Sen. Fred Thompson is playing the part of Clinton.
Dole and his handlers publicly stress they are up against a masterful speaker in Clinton, while privately they pray their man can establish himself in 90 minutes as a viable alternative.
"Everybody knows how good Clinton is on his feet, but I think Senator Dole's honesty, knowledge and integrity will show through," Thompson said.
